Ex-Tesla Engineer’s SE3 Raises $30M for Drone AI Built for Any Drone
Posted on November 13, 2026 November 12, 2026 by Flavia Moura
13
Nov
The Munich startup is the only serious bidder for the battlefield command screen that sells nothing underneath it. Ukraine approved a new drone model about every 10 hours this year. That is the whole pitch, and the whole problem.
SE3, a Munich spinout from the Technical University of Munich, raised a $30 million Series A led by Accel to build AI that runs drones from any manufacturer. The bet is that militaries will pay for neutrality as their fleets splinter. Ukraine codified 650 new drone systems in the first 265 days of 2026.
Picture a Bundeswehr operator in 2028. Her unit flies quadcopters from one German startup, fixed-wing scouts from another, loitering munitions from a third, and a couple of ground robots nobody remembers ordering. Each one shipped with its own app. Now she wants to say, out loud, “send something to look two kilometers north over that forest,” and have the right machine take off.
That sentence is the product SE3 is selling. The hard part is not the voice command. It is that the machine she wants could have been built by anyone.
What Happened
Fortune reported on November 12 that SE3, which recently dropped “Labs” from its name, closed a $30 million Series A led by Accel, with Keen, Lakestar and Seedcamp joining. Valuation, revenue and total funding were not disclosed.
The round lands fast. SE3 came out of stealth on June 26, 2026, with a €5.5 million seed (about $6.1 million) led by Lakestar, alongside Seedcamp, EWOR, the Sequoia Scout Fund and Plug and Play. That is roughly 4.9 times the seed check, raised 139 days later.
The basics:
Who: CEO Lukas Köstler, a former TUM PhD student who worked on Tesla’s Autopilot team and at Nvidia Research; CTO Simon Klenk, his TUM labmate; and chief science officer Daniel Cremers, who runs the computer vision lab the company spun out of.
What it builds: software that fuses video and sensor feeds from many drones and ground vehicles into one 3D map, labels what is in it, and lets soldiers query it or task machines by voice. It also builds onboard autonomy for navigation when GPS is jammed, object detection and swarm behavior.
Who pays: the Bundeswehr, under contracts to develop fleet command AI, plus Ukraine, where the technology is already deployed. Partners include sensor maker Hensoldt, drone software company Auterion and drone developer ERC.
What the money buys: headcount goes from about 40 to about 120, with new offices in London, Berlin, the Nordics and Baltics, and Poland.
Köstler described the shared map to Fortune as working “like a mini map, how you would know it from a strategy game.” Gamers will get it instantly. Procurement officers will get it the moment they price what happens when that mini map only shows one vendor’s units.
The Backstory
Every outlet will frame this as another European defense AI round riding rearmament money. True, and not very useful. The more interesting fact is the market structure SE3 is walking into.
Start with Ukraine, the world’s largest live test of drone procurement. Its Ministry of Defence codified 413 unmanned aerial systems in the first half of 2026, up more than 30% on the same period of 2025 and more than 73% on 2024. By September 22 the count was 650.
